newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh hill peace deal reached but not signed.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh hill peace deal reached but not signed.

text.p: Rebel tribal leaders on Thursday failed to sign a peace agreement to end a protracted insurgency in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, but instead flew to their base to brief the rank and file, officials said.
Officials were tight-lipped about when the tribal Shanti Bahini guerrilla leaders would return to Dhaka to formally sign the agreement, which was reached on Wednesday after four days of talks.

"We are coming again but when that will be (will be) decided later through contacts," chief rebel negotiator Jyotirindra Budhipriya Larma told reporters before leaving the meeting venue to board a military helicopter.
Larma, chief of the Shanti Bahini's political wing, and his team would be flying to Dudukchhari, a remote area in the Hill Tracts near the Indian border, officials said.
Chief government negotiator Abdul Hasanat Abdullah told reporters on Wednesday that both sides had reached agreement on all issues and would sign a peace deal soon.
"We have reached consensus on all issues. We are going to sign a peace deal very soon," he said.
Larma's departure from Dhaka on Thursday indicated that he would seek approval of the agreement by his tribal comrades and disciples before putting his signature on it.
Government negotiators said they would brief Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina about the outcome of the latest round of talks with the Shanti Bahini.
Government sources said on Thursday a signing date would be fixed in June.

"We are willing to make it before the budget session of parliament due in the second half of June," Mosharraf Hossain, ruling Awami League party legislator and member of the government negotiating team, told Reuters.
More than 8,500 civilians, rebels and soldiers have been killed since 1973 when the Shanti Bahini began the insurgency over demands for autonomy of the Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma.
The rebels had insisted that some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers be expelled from the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) region and the army be withdrawn.
How the issues were solved was not immediately known.

The local Independent newspaper, quoting an unnamed meeting source, reported on Thursday that both sides agreed the army would remain posted only in the main Hill Tract barracks, while Shanti Bahini guerrillas would lay down their arms.
The Benagli-speaking settlers would be relocated only on government land while the tribals would be given "constitutional recognition", the paper said.
The government has also agreed to form a special council in each of the three Hill Tract districts, the daily said. The council's function was not known.
The government has already started reclaiming tribal land and restoring it to thousands of tribal refugees who returned home in the first phase of a repatriation programme in March and April.
